{{DISPLAYTITLE:Hamilton's principle — Notation}}
{{Hamilton's principle map}}
This page fixes the symbols used across the volume and records where they collide
with the notation of the primary sources. It exists because three collisions in
this subject are severe enough to make a source unreadable if they are not
declared, and because a reader moving between this volume and Hamilton's essays
will meet all three within a page.

Independent variables are <math>x</math> in the mathematics tracks and
<math>t</math> where the subject is mechanics. Greek indices run over spacetime
coordinates; Latin indices over coordinates or fields.

== Collision 1: <math>V</math> ==

'''This is the collision that matters most, and it is the one that makes
Hamilton's essays unreadable if it is missed.'''

{| class="wikitable"
! symbol !! in this volume !! in Hamilton 1834
|-
| <math>V</math> || potential energy || the '''characteristic function''', <math>\int_0^t 2T\,dt</math>
|-
| <math>U</math> || not used || the '''force-function''', with sign opposite to potential energy
|-
| <math>T</math> || kinetic energy || half the living force; same quantity
|}

Hamilton's <math>V</math> is not a potential. It is the accumulated action, and
his law of living force reads <math>T = U + H</math> rather than
<math>T + V = E</math> because his <math>U</math> is minus the potential.

A reader who carries this volume's <math>V</math> into Hamilton's equation (A.)
will read it as nonsense. The quotations on
[[Hamilton's principle/Mathematics/Action as a function of its endpoints|Action as a function of its endpoints]] are
footnoted with this warning at each occurrence.

== Collision 2: the action itself ==

{| class="wikitable"
! quantity !! this volume !! Hamilton 1834 !! Hamilton 1835 !! common modern usage
|-
| <math>\int L\,dt</math> || <math>S</math> || — || <math>S</math> || <math>S</math>
|-
| <math>\int 2T\,dt = \int\sum p\,dq</math> || <math>W</math> || <math>V</math> || <math>V</math> || <math>S_0</math> or <math>W</math>
|}

Hamilton's first essay works entirely with the abbreviated action. The function
modern texts call the action enters only in the second essay, as a part of
<math>V</math> into which the time enters explicitly.

Both quantities are routinely called "the action" and both principles are
routinely called "the principle of least action". This volume writes
<math>S</math> and <math>W</math>, names the principles separately, and uses
''stationary'' rather than ''least'' for both. The distinction is the subject of
[[Hamilton's principle/Mathematics/Abbreviated action: Maupertuis versus Hamilton|Abbreviated action: Maupertuis versus Hamilton]].

== Collision 3: <math>\delta</math> ==

<math>\delta</math> carries three distinct meanings in the sources, and Hamilton
uses two of them on the same page.

{| class="wikitable"
! usage !! meaning !! where
|-
| <math>\delta J</math> || first variation of a functional || this volume, and Hamilton
|-
| <math>\delta y</math> || an infinitesimal change of path, this volume's <math>\varepsilon\eta</math> || classical literature, and Hamilton
|-
| <math>\delta V/\delta x</math> || '''partial derivative''' || Hamilton throughout, where a modern text writes <math>\partial V/\partial x</math>
|}

The third is the trap. In Hamilton's equations (C.), (D.), (E.), (F.) and (G.),
quoted on
[[Hamilton's principle/Mathematics/Action as a function of its endpoints|Action as a function of its endpoints]] and
[[Hamilton's principle/Mathematics/The Hamilton-Jacobi equation|the Hamilton-Jacobi equation]], every
<math>\delta</math> in a quotient is an ordinary partial derivative. Read as
variations they are meaningless.

This volume writes <math>\partial</math> for partial derivatives everywhere in
its own text and preserves Hamilton's <math>\delta</math> inside quotations, with
a footnote at each occurrence.

== Noether's notation ==

Her symbols are preserved where her equations are reproduced, on
[[Hamilton's principle/Mathematics/Noether's first theorem|Noether's first theorem]],
[[Hamilton's principle/Mathematics/Noether's second theorem|Noether's second theorem]] and
[[Hamilton's principle/Mathematics/Several independent variables|Several independent variables]].

{| class="wikitable"
! Noether !! meaning !! this volume's equivalent
|-
| <math>f</math> || the integrand || <math>\mathcal{L}</math>
|-
| <math>I</math> || the integral || <math>S</math>
|-
| <math>u_i</math> || dependent variables || fields <math>\phi_i</math>
|-
| <math>x_\lambda</math> || independent variables || <math>x^\alpha</math>
|-
| <math>\psi_i</math> || Lagrange expressions || left side of the Euler-Lagrange equation
|-
| <math>\mathrm{Div}\,A</math> || divergence || <math>\partial_\alpha A^\alpha</math>
|-
| <math>G_\rho</math> || finite continuous group, <math>\rho</math> parameters || global symmetry
|-
| <math>G_{\infty\rho}</math> || infinite continuous group, <math>\rho</math> arbitrary functions || gauge symmetry
|-
| <math>\Delta u</math> against <math>\delta u</math> || total change against change at fixed argument || see her equation (9)
|}

The last row is not a notational nicety. The two differ by
<math>\sum (\partial u/\partial x_\lambda)\Delta x_\lambda</math>, and compressing
them is where sign errors in derivations of Noether's theorem come from.

== Signs and units ==

Metric signature, where it appears, is <math>(+,-,-,-)</math>. Gravitational
acceleration is written <math>g_0</math> to avoid collision with the metric
determinant <math>g</math> and the metric components <math>g_{ik}</math>; the
collision is real and appears on
[[Hamilton's principle/Applications/The catenary|the catenary]] and
[[Hamilton's principle/Applications/The Einstein-Hilbert action|the Einstein-Hilbert action]] within the same
volume.

Equation numbers restart at (1) on each page and are written inside the
mathematics as <math>\qquad\qquad\mathrm{(n)}</math>, because MediaWiki's TeX
checker rejects the usual tagging command. The cross-page index is
[[Hamilton's principle/Equation index|Equation index]].

== A note on <math>\vert\;\vert</math> ==

Absolute values and norms are written with <math>\vert</math> rather than the
usual paired delimiters, throughout, for the same reason: the checker rejects the
paired forms. This is a constraint of the platform, not a convention of the
subject.
